headline: Claude can now send Gmail messages without human approval on paid plans
summary: Anthropic's AI assistant is gaining more autonomy in Google Workspace, with the ability to draft, reply to, and forward emails automatically.
details: Anthropic's AI assistant, Claude, is now capable of sending emails from Gmail without direct human oversight for paid users. This update expands Claude's integration with Google Workspace, allowing it to draft, reply to, and forward messages autonomously.

While the default setting requires user approval before sending, Team and Enterprise plan administrators can enable fully autonomous email actions for their members. This feature aims to streamline communication workflows by letting Claude handle routine email tasks.

Beyond Gmail, Claude also receives improved file management capabilities in Google Drive. It can now share, move, and trash files independently, though its access is limited to text content within files, excluding images or comments.

Users can opt out of these autonomous features through the chat interface, while organization owners can disable them via the 'Connectors' settings. Anthropic notes that performance may vary for large mailboxes and Claude cannot access email attachments.

headline_marked: Qualcomm [[retracts Snapdragon C power efficiency benchmarks]] after initial release
headline: Qualcomm retracts Snapdragon C power efficiency benchmarks after initial release
summary: The company updated benchmark slides, removing results for idle apps and web browsing nearly a week after their initial publication.
details: Qualcomm has issued an update to its benchmark slides for the new Snapdragon C chip, which targets laptops starting at $300. The company requested that publications replace the original slides, which included power efficiency benchmarks, with an updated version.

The updated slide omits two specific results: those related to idle apps and web browsing. A Qualcomm representative stated the change was made to "improve clarity and relevance," but the timing of the removal, nearly a week after the initial announcement, has raised questions.

This action constitutes a retraction of published benchmarks, carrying more weight than a simple update. While Qualcomm has not provided a reason beyond "improving clarity," the efficiency claims made for the Snapdragon C have now been altered.

The removed results were prefixed with "ABL," an acronym whose meaning is currently unclear. It is speculated to potentially stand for "all-day battery life" or a similar metric relevant to efficiency claims. Qualcomm has been asked for clarification on this acronym.

The benchmarks originally compared the Snapdragon C against Intel's N250 chip. Qualcomm's chip features eight Kryo CPU cores, while the N250 is a quad-core processor. The comparison was made on battery power, with Qualcomm stating the Intel machine's power was configured to match the larger screen size of the Snapdragon device.
